problem: Term drift: manners (moeurs) rendered as "manners" twice ("foreign manners", "the manners of the people"); STYLE-NOTE requires customs. Also minor: "It is like paintings" loosens the analogy; dropped "indeed".
replacement: Not only do the Americans constantly draw on the treasures of English literature, but it may truly be said that they find English literature growing on their own soil. Most of the small number of men in the United States who are engaged in writing literary works are English in substance, and still more so in form. Thus they carry into the midst of democracy the ideas and literary fashions current among the aristocratic nation they have taken as their model. They paint with colors borrowed from foreign customs, and since they hardly ever portray the country they were born in as it really is, they are seldom popular there. The citizens of the United States are themselves so convinced that books are not published for them that, before they can make up their minds about the merit of one of their authors, they generally wait until his fame has been confirmed in England, just as, in paintings, the author of an original is held to be entitled to judge the merit of a copy. The inhabitants of the United States, then, have at present, properly speaking, no literature. The only authors I acknowledge as American are the journalists. They are not, indeed, great writers, but they speak the language of their countrymen and make themselves heard by them. Other authors are foreigners. They are to the Americans what the imitators of the Greeks and Romans were to us at the revival of learning: an object of curiosity, not of general sympathy. They amuse the mind, but they do not act upon the customs of the people.

problem: "for every few great authors" is odd and changes the sense of "for some few great authors who adorn it" (the few great authors versus thousands of hacks).
replacement: In democratic periods the public often treats authors as kings treat their courtiers: they enrich them and they despise them. What more do the venal souls born in courts, or worthy of living there, need? Democratic literature is always infested with a tribe of writers who regard letters as a mere trade, and for the few great authors who adorn it, you may count thousands of idea-peddlers.
